about: Jane's own topics: added by this project, not part of the Marble Skill Taxonomy. Same schema as data/marble/topics.json. Ids start with jane_ (never mt_) so they can never collide with Marble ids, and they live outside data/marble/ so a Marble data refresh never touches them. build.mjs appends them after the Marble topics in public/tax.json. centrality is hand-set (Marble computes its own; the app does not use it). See data/jane/README.md.

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Compound growth
topics.description: Money that earns interest on its interest grows by the same percentage each period: future value = present value × (1 + rate)^years (FV = PV × (1+r)^n); why savings and investments grow along a curve that gets steeper over time, unlike simple interest, which adds the same amount each year
evidence: Work out year by year how $100 grows at 10% a year for 3 years, and explain why each year adds more than the last
Use FV = PV × (1 + r)^n to find the value of a saving after a given number of years
Compare simple and compound interest on the same amount and explain why the compound total pulls ahead
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saved $200 at 5% interest a year, could they work out how much it would be worth after 3 years, and explain why it grows faster each year?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: The Rule of 72
topics.description: A mental-math shortcut for compound growth: the years needed to double money are about 72 ÷ the yearly growth rate in percent; the same rule estimates how fast inflation halves what money can buy
evidence: Estimate how many years it takes money to double at 6%, 8% and 12% a year using 72 ÷ rate
Work backwards to find the growth rate needed to double money in a given number of years
Use the rule to estimate how long it takes 4% inflation to halve what a dollar buys
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a savings account pays 9% a year, could they estimate in their head how many years it would take the money to double?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Real return and inflation
topics.description: Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same money buys less; the real return is what savings grow by after inflation: (1 + rate) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1, roughly the rate minus the inflation rate
evidence: Explain what inflation is, using a price that has gone up over time
Estimate the real return when savings earn 5% and prices rise 3% (about 2%)
Use (1 + r) ÷ (1 + i) − 1 to find the exact real return and compare it with the r − i estimate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s savings earned 4% in a year when prices rose 6%, could they explain whether they can buy more or less than before, and by roughly how much?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Present value
topics.description: Money today is worth more than the same amount later, because today's money can grow; present value runs compound growth backwards: PV = FV ÷ (1 + rate)^years, to compare money at different times
evidence: Explain why $100 today is worth more than $100 in five years
Use PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n to find how much to save now to have a target amount later
Compare two offers paid at different times (for example $100 now or $110 next year) at a given interest rate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were offered $100 now or $120 in three years, could they use present value to decide which is the better deal when savings earn 8% a year?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: True average return (geometric mean)
topics.description: The fair average of yearly growth rates is the geometric mean: multiply the growth factors, take the nth root, then subtract 1; why +50% followed by −50% loses money even though the simple average of the rates is 0%
evidence: Show that $100 up 50% then down 50% ends at $75, and explain why the simple average of 0% is misleading
Turn yearly percentage changes into growth factors (like 1.2 and 0.9) and multiply them
Find the true average yearly return by taking the nth root of the product of the growth factors and subtracting 1
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw an investment go up 20% one year and down 20% the next, could they explain why it did not break even and work out its true average yearly return?
